title: The Bell Beneath Hollowmere
summary: The silver bell that keeps the marsh-mist out of Hollowmere has been stolen, and the mist is already curling around the doorframes.
author: Dungeon

phases.text: Grubnak rips the curtain from his throne and wraps it round his shoulders like a war-cape. "NOW the Mire King fights!"

village-green.title: Hollowmere, at dawn
village-green.text:
The village of Hollowmere squats at the marsh's edge like a hen over eggs. This morning the eggs are cracking: the silver bell is gone from its little shrine beneath the village oak, and without its toll the mist creeps in off the water, grey and patient, curling around the doorframes as if it owns them.

{{hero.name}} stands on the green while worried villagers go about their day badly — sweeping already-clean steps, fetching water they don't need, all for an excuse to glance at the marsh.

A hundred years the bell has rung at dusk. Last night it didn't, and nobody slept.

choices.text: Visit Mother Sedge, the marsh hermit

elder.title: Elder Bron
elder.speaker: elder-bron
elder.text:
"A hundred years that bell has tolled at dusk, and a hundred years the mist has kept to its side of the water. My grandmother swore the bell didn't chase it — it *asked* it back, politely, every evening. Mist respects good manners.

Last night someone — something — took it. Tracks lead east, into the marsh, and there's talk of a goblin band camped out that way under a mud-crowned chief.

Bring it back, {{hero.name}}, and Hollowmere will pay 150 gold and remember you kindly. Which is worth more, some days."

choices.text: "Where exactly would a thief take a bell?"

elder-clue.title: What the elder knows
elder-clue.speaker: elder-bron
elder-clue.text:
"Wolves range the marsh road — mind them. Hungry this time of year. If you keep your wits they may keep theirs; if not, well, you look like a meal.

Past the road there's a drowned chapel, halfway to nowhere. Our founders built it before the marsh ate the lower field. Beyond that is a goblin camp by the flooded crypt — they answer to some chief who calls himself the Mire King. Bells are shiny, and goblins are goblins.

Old Mother Sedge lives on a hummock off the road — half-hermit, half-witch, all trouble. She knows the marsh better than the mist does. Might be worth a visit, might be a wasted hour. Her moods run to weather."

shop.title: Pella's stall
shop.speaker: shopkeep-pella
shop.text:
"Adventuring gear, reasonably priced, only slightly damp! Potions, provisions, and one very lucky spoon.

Off to the marsh then? Take dried meat — wolves will follow a sausage anywhere, and it's a lot cheaper than dying."

choices.text: Buy a Potion of Healing (50 gp)
Buy dried meat for the road (5 gp)

smithy.title: The smithy
smithy.speaker: smith-tomas
smithy.text:
Tomas the smith is built like his own anvil and twice as cheerful. He turns a horseshoe on the fire and gives it a look of deep personal disappointment.

"Bell's gone, I hear. My grandfather's grandfather re-forged that bell the last time it cracked — took silver from three churches' worth of candelabra. Sacred metal, that. If goblins have it they'll have strung it up like a war-trophy, not melted it. Too proud of it.

You'll want your edge checked before you go? No charge for bell-rescuers."

choices.text: Tomas runs a thumb down your blade, corrects the grip in your hand without being asked, and sends you off feeling measurably more dangerous.

smithy-advice.title: Smith's advice
smithy-advice.speaker: smith-tomas
smithy-advice.text: "Three things. One: the marsh eats iron. Keep your blade oiled and wrapped when you can. Two: goblins are cowards one-to-one and heroes three-to-one — never let them count you. Three: the Mire King — if he's real — is still a goblin. Goblins deal. Find out what he wants that isn't a fight, and you might walk out with the bell and your skin both."

the-well.title: By the well
the-well.speaker: widle-of-the-well
the-well.text:
Widle of-the-well — so called because she never strays from it — intercepts you before your foot lands twice.

"The BELL? Oh yes, everyone knows. Wasn't the first thing to go missing, mind. Eda's pie went last week. And a goose. And — some say — the miller's cat, though the miller says the cat left voluntarily, which tells you everything about that household.

Now, about the marsh: everyone says 'goblins', but *I* heard the mist singing two nights before the bell went. Singing! Draw your own conclusions, {{hero.class}}."

choices.text: Listen closely — is she lying about the singing?

success.text: Her eyes go wet and far away when she mentions the singing. Whatever Widle heard, she believes every word — and it frightened her badly enough to repeat it.

failure.text: Widle talks the way water flows downhill — impossible to interrupt and ending where it wants anyway. You learn the goose's name (Maurice) and little else.

the-well-truth.title: One more thing
the-well-truth.speaker: widle-of-the-well
the-well-truth.text:
"And another thing — if you're going through the marsh, look for the lanterns. Mother Sedge hangs blue lanterns where the ground is firm. Blue light, safe ground; grey light, you sink. She taught me that when I was a girl, before she went strange.

Well. Stranger."

marsh-road.title: The marsh road
marsh-road.text:
The road is more of an apology than a road: planks over black water, reeds as tall as your shoulder, and a smell like yesterday's argument. Somewhere to the left a crow laughs at a joke only it understands.

There is a shorter way — the old causeway, drowned to the ankle, that the locals use when they're in a hurry. Finding it means reading the water. Blue lantern-light winks off to the right; grey haze sits everywhere else.

success.text: You find the old causeway, stones sitting just under the water's skin like a spine. Blue lantern-glow marks the good footing — Widle's tip was worth the goose story.

failure.text: The plank you choose is the wrong plank. You go knee-deep into marsh water that has opinions about visitors, and climb out heavier, wetter and humbler. No causeway in sight — you'll take the long way.

causeway-cross.title: The sunken causeway
causeway-cross.text:
The causeway is no wider than a roof-ridge and slick with weed. Below the water, pale shapes drift that you choose not to name. Ahead, the chapel bell-roof leans into view through the reeds.

Crossing dry-footed will take balance — or nerve.

success.text: You cross like a heron with somewhere to be, quick feet on slick stone, and gain the far bank dry as toast.

failure.text: Halfway across, a stone shifts and you meet the water. It's cold, it's personal, and something brushes your boot that you will not be discussing later. You haul out by the chapel's graveyard wall.

hermit-hut.title: Mother Sedge's hummock
hermit-hut.speaker: mother-sedge
hermit-hut.text:
A hut of woven willow sits on a dry knoll off the road, blue lanterns strung from its eaves. Mother Sedge herself is small, grey-wrapped, and stirring a pot that smells of moss and intent.

"{{hero.name}}," she says without turning, which is unsettling. "Come for the bell, like the mist said you would. The mist tells me things. Lies, mostly, but consistent ones.

The Mire King took it — not for its ring, child. For its silence. A bell that doesn't toll keeps the mist free to wander where it pleases. My knee hurts something cruel this week, or I'd have fetched it myself and saved everyone the worry."

success.text: Your fingers find the angry joint quickly enough. She hisses, then sighs like a kettle coming off the boil. "Competent hands. Rare, that." She looks at you properly for the first time, and her eyes are kinder than her reputation.

failure.text: You prod the joint; she yelps and smacks your knuckles with the ladle. "Hands like a troll's wedding. Fine — I'll do it myself." Despite the fuss, she seems faintly pleased someone tried.

choices.text: Ask plainly what the Mire King fears

success.text: "Plainly! Refreshing. Very well." She taps her ladle against the pot. "The boy is a magpie with a crown. Take that away and he's just noise."

failure.text: "Asking plainly gets you a plain answer: he fears nothing. Fearing takes imagination, and he spent all of his on the crown."

hermit-favour.title: The hermit's price
hermit-favour.speaker: mother-sedge
hermit-favour.text:
Mother Sedge rummages in a basket and produces a charm of woven sedge strung with a bead of river-moonstone, pale as a thumbnail.

"Moon-ward, the old priest called these — he made them before he went holy-mad and wandered off. Grubnak believes them *powerful*. He was raised on chapel stories, poor lamb: moon-charms frighten him half to death. Show him that, and even if it's as magical as a teacup, you'll have his attention.

Take a poultice too. You'll need it or you won't, but either way it's off my shelf."

wolf-approach.title: Eyes in the reeds
wolf-approach.text:
Three lean shapes detach themselves from the reeds and fan out across the road — marsh wolves, ribs showing through winter coats, hunger in their posture like a taut bowstring. They haven't charged yet. They're deciding whether you're worth the teeth.

The lead wolf's ears twitch at every reed-creak. Whatever decides this, it will be fast.

choices.text: Speak low and steady — calm the pack

success.text: You let your voice drop into the register of pack and patience — the sound their mothers made before they knew fear. The lead wolf holds your gaze a long moment, reading something you can't see yourself. Then, all at once, the three of them melt back into the reeds like grey water.

failure.text: The lead wolf flattens its ears. Whatever register you hit, it was the wrong one — perhaps 'lunch'. Diplomacy is over.

choices.text: You lob the meat wide of the road. Three muzzles turn as one — wolves will follow food anywhere, and Pella's dried meat is, apparently, exactly that. You walk on unmolested, smelling faintly of sausage.
Draw your weapon and stand your ground

wolf-fight.title: The pack charges
wolf-fight.text: The lead wolf commits, and the others follow — three grey streaks through the reeds, all teeth and trajectory. No more deciding.

victory.text: The last wolf limps yelping into the marsh. The road is yours — for what a marsh road is worth.

flee.text: You back away slowly, and the wolves, satisfied, let you. Hollowmere feels very quiet on the walk back.

dragged-clear.title: Dragged clear
dragged-clear.text:
You wake on the green at dusk. The miller found you on the road and dragged you home — his price is a modest lecture and your boots being full of marsh.

The mist is a little thicker tonight, curling round the well like it has questions.
dragged-clear.epilogue: The bell is still out there somewhere. So are your boots' warmth.

chapel.title: The drowned chapel
chapel.text:
The chapel leans out of the marsh like a drunk on a fencepost, its stones green to the waist. Inside, the pews have rotted to lace, and light falls through the collapsed roof in pale pillars onto the altar stone.

Something glints beneath the altar's lip. Above it, carved into the wall in a hand that cared deeply about getting it right, is an inscription — and beneath it, a small riddle-box of weathered wood.

success.text: Under the altar's lip, wrapped in oilcloth: the bell's silver clapper — and a scratched confession: *took the bell for the Mire King, gods forgive me, the mist sings to him now. I traded my penance for his protection.*

failure.text: You find only damp, a family of unimpressed frogs, and the sense that whatever was hidden here has walked off — recently, judging by the tracks heading deeper into the marsh. The carving on the wall, at least, isn't going anywhere.

success.text: Beneath the moss, runes: not a blessing but an *instruction*. Whoever built this place knew the marsh would come for it eventually — and prepared accordingly.

failure.text: The runes might as well be decorative moss. You make out one word — *ward* — before the pattern dissolves into nonsense.

chapel-carving.title: The chapel wall
chapel-carving.text:
The inscription, cleaned of moss, reads: *When the mist walks free, the bell must ring. When the bell is taken, ward the moon.*

Below it sits a riddle-box of weathered wood, still sealed after all these years — a small stone disc painted with a crescent moon turns on its face. The mechanism wants a specific answer.

success.text: You turn the crescent through its phases, matching each to a scratched rune — and the box clicks open like a sigh. Inside, wrapped in dry wool after all these years: a moon-ward charm, silver-bright.

failure.text: You work the crescent back and forth until your fingers ache. The box stays shut, smug as a banker.

choices.text: Ward-script — you studied this. Old Hollowmere liturgy, first-era. You turn the crescent to the waning phase the rune demands, and the box opens like it had been waiting politely.

chapel-charm.title: The moon-ward
chapel-charm.text: Inside the box, a charm of woven sedge and moonstone — twin to the kind the old marsh-hermits carry. Goblins raised on chapel stories believe these things burn holes in shadows.

chapel-loot.title: The altar's cache
chapel-loot.text: Alongside the clapper, the thief — or a penitent priest — left a small dry bundle of supplies tucked where the water couldn't reach.

lookout-approach.title: The goblin lookout
lookout-approach.speaker: goblin-lookout-npc
lookout-approach.text:
A lone goblin sits on a stump before a rope bridge, sharpening a fish knife with great ceremony and zero skill. A second stump nearby suggests he occasionally has company. Today it's just him, a dragonfly he's arguing with, and the bridge that leads to the camp.

"No passage!" he squeaks at your approach. "Bridge is for the Mire King's court only. Unless you're, um. Guests. Very important guests. Which you're obviously not, on account of not having a gift."

success.text: Skritch snaps a salute so sharp he nearly drops his knife. "Court's that way, your importances. Mind the third board — it's a traitor." He even holds the rope rail for you.

failure.text: Skritch squints. "Nope. Guests bring *cake*." He whistles shrilly — and answers himself with drawn steel.

success.text: You ghost through the reeds while Skritch argues with the dragonfly — the argument is going badly for him, which helps you. The rope bridge creaks once, politely, and lets you pass.

failure.text: Your foot finds the one loud reed in the marsh. Skritch spins round, knife first, offended in a deeply personal way.

success.text: You launch into 'Gobbo the Gobble' in passable Goblin. Skritch drops his knife and joins the second verse — he knows the harmony, the harmony knows him. By the third verse he's waving you over the bridge like an old friend. "Tell the King Skritch sent ye!" he calls after you. "He'll hate that!"

failure.text: Your Goblin is a dialect too far south, and it shows. Skritch listens politely, wincing at the chorus, then draws. "Nobody sings it *that* bad. Intruder!"

choices.text: "Let me pass, or this ends badly for you."

success.text: You let the weight of it sit in your voice. Skritch looks at you, at the knife, at you again, and makes the correct decision. "Bridge is right there, friend. Always was." He waves you through with a grin that is mostly fear.

failure.text: Skritch puffs up, which given his size is still not very up. "The Mire King says NOBODY passes! And Skritch obeys the King!" He whistles for help.

lookout-fight.title: Bridge guards
lookout-fight.text: Skritch yells for help and gets it — two raiders pile out of a reed hovel, blades first, looking entirely too eager.

victory.text: The raiders splash into the marsh and swim for it, still arguing about whose fault this was. Skritch is gone — the lookout has abandoned his post with impressive speed.

flee.text: You retreat over the causeway, arrows — well, pots — falling around you.

defeat.text: A pot, a flash of fire, and then nothing.

crypt-approach.title: The flooded crypt
crypt-approach.text:
Beyond the bridge the ground rises onto a hummock crowned by a sunken mausoleum — and ahead, strung between two dead willows, hangs the strangest sight in the marsh: a rough log palace with a throne visible through the doorway, and above it, on a gibbet of woven reeds, the bell of Hollowmere.

It hangs silent, catching what little light the marsh allows. Even at a distance, {{hero.name}} can see it's not been melted or defiled — just… hung. A trophy.

The crypt stairs gape darkly to your left. Something glitters down there. So do the bones. And a reed-bed runs around the back of the camp — thin cover, but cover.

success.text: The pool's surface isn't quite still. Something in it is breathing — slowly, wrong-footedly, like it's pretending to be a rock and doing a poor job.

failure.text: Just a pool. Probably. You move on, telling yourself the water's breathing is none of your business.

choices.text: Sneak round the reed-bed to the camp's back door
Go straight to the Mire King's door

bog-lurker-scene.title: The bog's tenant
bog-lurker-scene.text: The 'rock' unfolds itself: a bog-lurker, all mud and malice, hauling itself up out of the pool with a sound like a curse.

victory.text: The lurker collapses back into its pool with a sound of deep regret. Under a half-sunk stone it was guarding: a marsh pearl the size of a robin's egg.

flee.text: You back away from the pool. The lurker watches you go with the deep satisfaction of a thing that has won by default.

defeat.text: Mud, claws, cold water — then nothing.

bog-loot.title: The lurker's hoard
bog-loot.text: A bog-lurker's treasures: half a marsh pearl, and a lurker scale hard as flint.

reed-sneak.title: The back way
reed-sneak.text: The reed-bed is thin cover but the goblin camp's back has no watch — the Mire King keeps his eyes front, where the threats are supposed to come from. Wading through will take quiet feet and quieter breathing.

success.text: You slip through the reeds like a rumour. One goblin sentry walks past within arm's reach, humming tunelessly, and never looks down.

failure.text: A reed snaps under your knee like a firework. You freeze, hold your breath, and wade the last stretch while a sentry peers vaguely your way and decides the marsh made the noise. You're in — but soaked and rattled.

crypt-fight.title: Bones of the crypt
crypt-fight.text: The dead of Hollowmere's founders do not appreciate visitors. Two skeletons rise from the flooded niches, all jaw and grievance, rust-blades held with the easy confidence of things that have nothing left to lose.

victory.text: The last skull rolls down the steps and comes to rest, looking — if skulls can look — mildly embarrassed.

flee.text: You back out of the crypt, bones clattering disapprovingly behind you.

defeat.text: The bones are very thorough. You wake later, outside.

crypt-loot.title: The founders' rest
crypt-loot.text: In the driest niche, a founder's coffer — and beside it, a bone charm carved with the same ward-script as the chapel. Someone protected this place once.

boss-door.title: The Mire King's court
boss-door.speaker: grubnak
boss-door.text:
Grubnak, the Mire King, lounges on a throne of driftwood draped in marsh-silk, a crown of bottle-green glass on his head. A troll the size of a haystack dozes beside him, one eye open, one massive hand draped over the arm of the throne.

"Kneel," the king says grandly, "or don't — the floor's wet anyway. You want the bell? It's *my* bell now. It sings to the mist, and the mist sings back. Beautiful. Haunting. Mine.

You can offer something better, or you can fight the troll. Choose wisely — the troll hasn't lost in weeks."

choices.text: Reason with him — the mist will drown them too

success.text: You talk of shared roads and shared drownings, of a king who rules mud versus a neighbour who rules respect. Grubnak's eyes glisten behind the glass crown. "...The mist DOES get in everything," he admits at last. "Gets in the throne. Gets in the food. Gets in the *dignity*."

failure.text: "Poetry," sneers the king, "but I have a troll." He snaps his fingers.

choices.text: "Hand it over, or we take the crown too."

success.text: You let the promise hang in the air like storm-light. The troll opens its other eye, weighs you up with something that might be professional respect, and goes deliberately back to sleep. Grubnak deflates. "Fine. FINE. A king knows when a deal is a deal."

failure.text: Grubnak laughs until the crown rattles. "Take it? TAKE it?! Maul them, lads."

choices.text: You lift the clapper, and it catches the grey light. Grubnak goes very still. "That... that was my penance, little one. The priest took it for safe-keeping, before he went mad in the mist." He sighs, small and muddy. "A bell without a voice is just a bucket. Take it — take it home. Just tell them the Mire King was *magnanimous*."

You raise the charm, and it catches the marsh-light — silver-bright, old as the chapel. Grubnak's eyes go wide as saucers behind the crown. He knows what it is; more importantly, he *believes* what it is. "Put that away— put it AWAY," he hisses. "Take the bell. Take it and take the charm and go, before the moon-ward does whatever moon-wards do to kings of goblins."
Invoke your oath — this mist cannot stand

success.text: You speak your oath like a drawn blade, and the marsh seems to listen. Grubnak, raised on chapel stories and fireside warnings, recognises the cadence of a paladin's vow — and more importantly, recognises what it costs to break one. "A sworn oath," he mutters. "Can't argue with a sworn oath. Take it."

failure.text: Grubnak tilts his head, unimpressed by holy pronouncements. "Sworn oaths. Very dramatic. The troll doesn't believe in oaths." He waves you toward the troll like a tour guide.

boss-fight.title: The court of the Mire King
boss-fight.text: The troll unfolds to its full height — easily twice yours. Grubnak leaps from his throne, crownblade singing. There is nowhere left to run — not that you were planning to.

victory.text: The Mire King's crown rolls to a stop against your boot. His court has melted into the reeds. The bell hangs above you, quiet, waiting to go home.

defeat.text: The last thing you see is the troll's fist. The first thing you feel, later, is rope.

bell-recovered.title: The bell is yours
bell-recovered.text:
You cut the silver bell down from its reed gibbet. It's heavier than it looks — bells always are — and cool to the touch, as if it remembers every dusk it ever rang.

On the road back, a merchant's wagon squelches up beside you. The driver eyes the bell, then your scars, then the bell again, and makes an offer that's honestly quite flattering. Marsh-silver, he says, fetches a pretty price on the coast.

Hollowmere's smoke is just visible over the rise.

choices.text: Carry the bell home to Hollowmere
Sell the bell to the merchant (150 gp)

victory-ending.title: The bell rings out
victory-ending.text:
At dusk the silver bell tolls over Hollowmere for the first time in days, and the mist — insulted, outmanoeuvred, and thoroughly told — retreats back across the water in sulky grey ropes.

Elder Bron counts out 150 gold with wet eyes and pretends he isn't crying. Pella gives you a pie and a discount for life. Widle has already told everyone the bell rang itself — but she's also told them your name, and she says it like a hero's.
victory-ending.epilogue: Your name gets added to the shrine's little plaque. You are, officially, a friend of the village forever — and Mother Sedge sends word that the mist tells her you did well. From Mother Sedge, that's practically a parade.

peace-ending.title: A muddy peace
peace-ending.text:
The bell is handed down to you by the Mire King himself, with a short speech about neighbourly relations that nobody quite believes and everybody applauds anyway.

You ring it at dusk over Hollowmere. Somewhere out on the marsh, a goblin king listens — and, so the story goes, does not come again. The mist stays where it belongs. Mostly.
peace-ending.epilogue: You saved the bell without drawing a blade. The bards will be insufferable about it, and you'll enjoy every insufferable word.

sell-ending.title: A fair price
sell-ending.text:
Gold is gold, and 150 of it weighs pleasantly in your hand as the wagon rolls away with Hollowmere's bell in the back, bound for some collector on the coast who probably deserves it less than the village did.

The mist keeps rolling in over Hollowmere. You tell yourself they can buy another bell. You tell yourself that quite a lot, actually.
sell-ending.epilogue: Somewhere, a shrine stands empty. Somewhere else, a merchant makes a tidy profit. You try not to think about the crow laughing in the reeds.

captured-ending.title: The Mire King's guest
captured-ending.text:
You wake tied to a throne-room post while the court of the Mire King argues about whether you count as 'a guest' or 'a larder'. Grubnak, magnanimous in victory, settles it: you are thrown out of the marsh with a warning, a bruise, and most of your dignity intact.

The bell keeps singing to the mist. For now.
captured-ending.epilogue: You limp home. The elder doesn't say 'I told you so', which somehow makes it worse. Mother Sedge sends a poultice and a note that just says: *next time, try the charm.*
